\section[o equívoco]{o equívoco — the misunderstanding, the mistake}

\label{lesson:PT-C343-equivoco}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for credible, then the Portuguese for to claim.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o equívoco}
\textbf{o equívoco} — \textquotedblleft{}the misunderstanding, the mistake\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Houve um equívoco: eu disse terça, não quinta.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{There was a misunderstanding: I said Tuesday, not Thursday.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Por equívoco} — by mistake. As an adjective, ambiguous: \emph{uma frase equívoca}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{equívoco} is a learned borrowing from Late Latin \emph{aequivocus} \textquotedblleft{}of like significations, ambiguous\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), built on \emph{aequus} \textquotedblleft{}equal\textquotedblright{} and \emph{vocāre} \textquotedblleft{}to call\textquotedblright{}: one name that calls two things.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o equívoco}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{o equívoco}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{o equívoco}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for credible, then the Portuguese for to claim, then say \emph{o equívoco} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does o equívoco mean? (\textquotedblleft{}The misunderstanding, the mistake\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[esclarecer]{esclarecer — to clarify, to clear up}

\label{lesson:PT-C343-esclarecer}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to claim, then the Portuguese for the misunderstanding.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: esclarecer}
\textbf{esclarecer} — \textquotedblleft{}to clarify, to clear up\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Quero esclarecer uma coisa antes de começar.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{I want to clarify one thing before I start.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Esclarecer uma dúvida} — to clear up a doubt.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{esclarecer} is built in Portuguese from \emph{claro} \textquotedblleft{}clear\textquotedblright{}, inherited from Latin \emph{clārus} \textquotedblleft{}bright, clear\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), with \emph{es-} and the verb ending \emph{-ecer}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Portuguese for to claim, then the Portuguese for the misunderstanding, then say \emph{esclarecer} again

\section[o esclarecimento]{o esclarecimento — the clarification}

\label{lesson:PT-C343-esclarecimento}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the misunderstanding, then the Portuguese for to clarify.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: o esclarecimento}
\textbf{o esclarecimento} — \textquotedblleft{}the clarification\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
O professor deu um esclarecimento sobre o exame.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The teacher gave a clarification about the exam.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Pedir esclarecimentos} — to ask for clarification.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{esclarecimento} is built on \emph{esclarecer} \textquotedblleft{}to clarify\textquotedblright{} with \emph{-mento}; the verb rests on \emph{claro}, inherited from Latin \emph{clārus} \textquotedblleft{}bright, clear\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.

\section[sublinhar]{sublinhar — to stress, to emphasise; to underline}

\label{lesson:PT-C343-sublinhar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for to clarify, then the Portuguese for the clarification.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: sublinhar}
\textbf{sublinhar} — \textquotedblleft{}to stress, to emphasise; to underline\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
A médica sublinhou que é preciso descansar.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{The doctor stressed that rest is needed.}
\end{quote}

Literally to draw a line under a word; figuratively to stress a point.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{sublinhar} is built from \emph{sub-} \textquotedblleft{}under\textquotedblright{} and \emph{linha} \textquotedblleft{}line\textquotedblright{}, which is inherited from Latin \emph{līnea} \textquotedblleft{}a linen thread, a string, a line\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short).
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\section[salientar]{salientar — to point out, to highlight}

\label{lesson:PT-C343-salientar}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Portuguese for the clarification, then the Portuguese for to stress.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: salientar}
\textbf{salientar} — \textquotedblleft{}to point out, to highlight\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Ela salientou que o hotel fica perto da praia.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{She pointed out that the hotel is near the beach.}
\end{quote}

Close to \emph{sublinhar}: \emph{é de salientar que…} — it is worth pointing out that…

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{salientar} is built on \emph{saliente} \textquotedblleft{}prominent\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), from Latin \emph{saliēns}, the present participle of \emph{salīre} \textquotedblleft{}to leap, to jump\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short): what jumps out at you.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}
